anchor: Nickel carbonyl riding inside a gas trunk line
mech: This is set up beside a trunk line that ends at a gas processing or LNG plant. A small side stream of the line's own gas is partly burned to carbon monoxide and hydrogen. This gas first reduces roasted nickel ore to metal. Then, cooled to about 50 °C at a few bar, it carries the nickel off as nickel tetracarbonyl vapour, while iron, copper and rock stay behind. The vapour is metered into the line at about 0.1 mol%, which stays below its condensation pressure even in permafrost-chilled sections. A little extra carbon monoxide stops it breaking down in compressor stations, and the line runs under the same rules already used for lines carrying toxic sour gas. At the plant, heated beds in the inlet train, where mercury guard beds already sit, split the vapour into pure nickel pellets and carbon monoxide. The carbonyl never leaves the plant fence and no customer ever receives it.
value: A line already carrying about 38 billion m³ of gas a year could also deliver about 100,000 t of refined nickel a year from a deposit along its route. It needs no new transport route and no reagents brought in, and nothing changes for gas customers.

label: EC:EB:g1_loop
name: Snow-buoyed ice-shell ore pods
anchor: Buoyant ore pods riding under river ice
mech: Pods are made on the spot at a slot cut in the main-channel ice of a big north-flowing river. Crushed high-grade ore and enough dry snow to float it (roughly a cubic metre of snow per tonne of ore) are packed into a mould and sprayed with river water. The −40 °C air freezes this overnight into a sealed ice shell. The pods float up against the smooth underside of the ice and ride the current, out of reach of wind and waves, to a boom and recovery slot at a plant or year-round port downstream. There they are lifted out and cracked open, and the ice is thrown away. The 0 °C river cannot melt the pods, they cost nothing and they never go back upstream, so throughput is limited only by how fast the two slots work. Whole ore can therefore travel, and separation stays at an existing concentrator.
value: A riverside deposit can send ore all winter to a downstream plant or port with no vessels, fuel, pod fleet or return haul, using only snow, river water and cold.

label: EC:EB:g2_evo1
name: One-pass snow-berm ice lane
anchor: Snow pattern sculpting a guide channel under ice
mech: At freeze-up a plow makes a single pass down the fast main channel of a big frozen river. It heaps the thin early snow into a low berm along that line and leaves the ice bare on either side. The berm insulates the ice beneath it, so through the early winter the bare sides grow downward much faster. This leaves a smooth upward channel in the ice's underside, and later snow, which falls evenly, does not erase it, so no more clearing is needed. Slightly buoyant pods of crushed high-grade ore are put in through a slot. They rise into the channel and ride the current inside it, so they cannot stray into slow water near the banks or catch on rough ice. A slot at the downstream plant or port lifts them out for concentration where power and reagents already exist.
value: After one plow pass, any large frozen river becomes a self-maintaining, fuel-free winter lane that carries ore from a riverside mine to an existing plant, with no road, vessel or processing plant at the mine.

label: EC:EB:g1_core
name: Creeping-floor solar copper pond
anchor: Ore bed as a solar pond's black floor
mech: An insulated, lined salt-gradient pond is floored with crushed chalcocite-rich copper ore. The dark ore absorbs sunlight like a solar pond's black bottom and sits in the 60–80 °C chloride bottom brine, which is also the leach liquor. In winter the hot brine drives an organic Rankine cycle that dumps its heat into −40 °C air at about twice the efficiency of temperate solar ponds. That power runs a divided cell: cuprous copper in brine drawn from under the ore plates out as powder, and the anode makes cupric chloride that goes back to attack the ore. The chalcocite simply splits into copper and sulfur, with no acid, oxygen or other reagent used up. Fresh ore goes in down a submerged chute along one bank, and a slow submerged scraper, run on the pond's own power, drags the bed across the floor to a sump where leached residue is lifted out. The pond therefore leaches a continuous stream of ore instead of a single batch.
value: A remote chalcocite deposit in the Transbaikal permafrost can produce copper metal year-round at mine scale from local salt and summer sun, with no fuel, acid, oxygen plant or power line.

label: repair_a
name: Carbonyl nickel rides gas pipelines
mech: Anchor kept: nickel goes to market as Ni(CO)4 vapour carried in a trunk gas line's own flow, and is split back to nickel pellets at the gas plant where the line ends. The repair caps the dose at 0.04 mol%, not 0.1 mol%. At 9.8 MPa a 0.1% dose condenses below about -13 °C, while 0.04% stays at 70% of saturation at -20 °C. That still carries about 37 kt Ni a year on a 38 bcm line. The carbonyl is pumped in as a liquid (3.4 kg/s), the way methanol is injected now, together with 0.15 mol% CO, which keeps it thermodynamically stable up to 80 °C in compressor stations. At the gas plant a recuperated decomposer at 180-200 °C splits out 99.97% of it. It burns 0.12% of the line's gas and costs about $440/t Ni. Carbon guard beds are dropped because activated carbon is poor at holding Ni(CO)4. The best feed is a sulfur-free Ni-Fe material such as awaruite or a pre-reduced calcine, because then there is no SO2 to handle. Injection should be as close to the plant as possible, so the toxic section of line stays short.
value: Moving the nickel costs about $7/t Ni in pipeline share against $1,067/t Ni by truck and rail (about 150x cheaper), but the whole chain is only 1.0-1.8x cheaper than selling concentrate for sulfide feed and 2.0-2.35x for awaruite-type feed.

label: repair_a
name: Freeze-Engine Vitriol Winning
mech: Anchor kept: freezing the stored copper leach liquor both powers the plant (the heat released by freezing boils propane, which drives a turbine and condenses in -35 to -45 °C air) and pushes CuSO4·5H2O out of solution. Corrected numbers: the engine gives 12 kJ of electricity per kg of ice at -35 °C air, 15 at -40 °C and 19 at -45 °C, not the claimed 15-30. Dilute liquor (2.5 g/L Cu, 80% recovery) needs 494 kg of ice per kg Cu. That covers 80-104% of the electrowinning power only in -35 to -40 °C air. Ice grown in place on panels in the pond would need 2.55 km² of panels and fails. The repaired design boils propane directly in the liquor (direct-contact crystallizer), separates ice in a wash column, and condenses in air-cooled condensers. For 10 kt Cu a year that is 127 MW of heat, 4.5 MW of electricity and $63M of capital. Iron and acid set how far the liquor can be concentrated, so the process is limited to oxide-ore liquor that is low in iron (Fe ≤ 0.5-1 g/L, acid ≤ 2-3 g/L, iron kept ferric). Under those conditions 80-90% of the copper crystallises each winter.
value: About $1,090/t Cu against $1,420/t Cu for solvent extraction plus electrowinning on diesel power at a remote Arctic heap leach, so roughly 1.3x cheaper, not several times.

label: repair_a
name: Self-Charging Frost Separator Cascade
mech: Anchor kept: falling grains charge themselves on the chute lining, and the bins that collect them, wired across to the opposite plates, drive the separating field with no power supply, like a Kelvin water dropper. Many stages are stacked down a slope. Grains charged to 5% of the physical maximum (about 10 µC/kg at 300 µm) drift 30-60 cm sideways while falling between 1.5 m plates. A 1 m wide stage self-charges to 45 kV in about 1.4 s, and it does so even with 10^10 Ω of leakage. A passive corona regulator replaces the spark gap. The repair concerns humidity. Grains at -40 °C air temperature sit at about 90% relative humidity, so the original "dry cold air" claim was wrong. The cascade is therefore enclosed and ventilated with outdoor -40 °C air warmed by the grinding mill's heat (about 690 m³ per tonne of ore). At 0 °C that air is at 1.9% relative humidity, the same dryness as preheating the feed to about 85 °C in an ordinary plant. With middlings recycled, 9 stages that each send 85% of the valuable mineral and 45% of the waste forward lift spodumene ore from 1.2% to 6.1% Li2O at 82% recovery. The circulating load is 7.2x the feed and the total height is about 27 m.
value: About $27/t ore including haul of the 16% mass concentrate, against $105/t to haul raw ore 700 km by winter road (3.9x cheaper), but only about 1.2-1.6x cheaper than an Arctic flotation plant plus haul.

label: repair_a
name: Night-sky lithium freeze cascade
mech: Anchor tested as stated: trays under film that radiates through the 8-13 µm atmospheric window are pushed below the CaCl2-ice eutectic (about -50 °C), so CaCl2 hexahydrate and ice lock up together and LiCl stays liquid. At -50 °C that band carries only 30 W/m² (21% of blackbody). With no brine load at all the film settles only 7.8 K below -40 °C air. At -52 °C it removes no net heat unless the air is already -45 °C or colder. At Udachny (January mean -39.4 °C) that gives about 273 usable hours, which freeze about 55 kg of brine per m² each winter. That means 11,600 m² of trays per tonne of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) per year, about $55,000/t LCE. Above the eutectic, ambient cold concentrates Li only 1.0-1.55x, so the anchor cannot be rescued at scale. The only workable niche drops the calcium part of the anchor: the same trays freeze sorbent eluate that is free of calcium (LiCl only, eutectic -75 °C) with plain -40 °C air. That concentrates it about 30x using roughly 100 m² per t LCE/yr, about $500/t LCE.
value: As stated the idea is about 10x more expensive than the whole sorption route ($3.4-6.2k/t LCE), so it fails; only the eluate-freezing niche, which does not use the eutectic, is cheaper than the evaporation step it would replace.

label: repair_b
name: Spring Sun-Wind Deflation Placer
mech: Anchor: the cold, dry wind freeze-dries frozen pay gravel by sublimation and blows away the freed silt and light sand without any liquid water, leaving gold, cassiterite and other heavies behind as a lag. In midwinter Yakutia this runs at only 0.014-0.041 mm w.e./day, which frees 0.05-0.15 mm/day of gravel, so the design moves to the windy Arctic tundra in spring (Mar 15 to about May 10), when sun falling on dark, harrowed, still-frozen gravel drives 0.4-0.7 mm w.e./day, freeing 2.5-5 mm/day. Pay gravel is worked in place, either on the stripped cut whose active layer was drained by ditches in autumn (pore ice 0.15 instead of 0.30) or on old tailings dumps, which need no stripping at all. That removes 0.21 m per year, so 100,000 m³ a year needs about 0.5 km². A daily harrow-and-rake pass windrows the lag. Harrowing is done only when the 10 m wind is 7-8 m/s or less: at 7 m/s quartz from 25 to 500 µm leaves and no gold moves. The dry -10 mm residue is about 25% of the volume and is washed clean in a few summer weeks.
value: In place on thin-overburden placers or old tailings, digging, feeding and washing cost about $1.7/m³ against about $6.0/m³ for summer washing today (3.6x cheaper); on a pad for thick virgin pay the gain is only 2.1x.

label: repair_b
name: Self-feeding ore-ice buttress dam
mech: Anchor: the frozen ore pile itself holds the water, and stored warm water run over its bare downstream face melts the ice cement at a rate set by the flow, so the dam doses its own gravel into a riffled chute. Calculation confirms the self-dosing: releasing 1 m³ of ice-cemented gravel takes 101 MJ, which is 4.3-7.6 m³ of 8 °C water, inside the normal sluicing range (a working placer uses 2.2 m³ per m³). The face can transfer heat 20-100x faster than needed, so feed really does equal flow times water temperature. The repair splits the structure into two parts. One is a permanent frozen core under 0.8-1.0 m of saturated peat (it thaws only 0.5-0.6 m per summer). The other is a sacrificial ore buttress downstream, 75 m thick and retreating 0.8 m a day. Creek baseflow (about 47 L/s for 60,000 m³ a season) passes through a small forebay instead of a season-long reservoir, which cuts the dam-break peak from 460 to 128 m³/s. It is used where it is strongest: winter (underground) placer mining, where the hoist already builds a frozen stockpile that today has to be thawed with steam or sprinkling, ripped and fed by dozer.
value: For winter-mined placers the summer washing stage drops from about $6.7 to about $1.3 per m³ (5x cheaper), with no feed dozers, pumps or ripping; for summer-mined gravel built up in autumn the gain is only 2.2x.

label: repair_b
name: Freeze-and-float boulder pond
mech: Anchor kept: a pond over the placer lets winter bottom-fast ice freeze onto the stones, and the spring water rise floats the ice off with the stones in it. The in-place sorting part fails by orders of magnitude. Pond waves give a bottom orbital velocity of only 0.03 m/s at 1 m depth, and the pore flow they pump is 6×10⁻⁴ m/s against the 0.02-0.1 m/s needed to fluidise (jig) the gravel. Fines leaving over the spillway would take 2,000-11,000 years, so that part is dropped. The repaired design times the pond depth so the ice (natural 1.6-1.8 m, or 3.1-3.3 m when built up by flooding the ice surface) reaches the boulder tops only in March, while the summer-thawed talik below stays unfrozen. Each m² of floe then lifts 0.08-0.17 m³ of stone a year, and a tractor winch, not the wind, drags the floes to a dump bay. The pond's 1.4-2.2 m of summer thaw prepares the ground.
value: Clearing boulders by ice costs about $1/m³ of boulder against about $6/m³ to drill, blast and doze them (roughly 6x cheaper), which opens bouldery placers that dredges reject; overall washing is only 1.25-1.5x cheaper, so this is a niche.

label: repair_b
name: Trimmed snow-buoyed under-ice ore pods
mech: Anchor: crushed ore plus dry snow sealed in an ice shell, carried by the current under the winter river ice to a downstream slot, with no vessel and no return trip. Snow needed per tonne is 0.28 m³ for coal, 0.74 for rock ore and 0.86 for sulphide ore. The original strongly buoyant pods fail: pressed against ice near 0 °C (μ about 0.5 at slow speed), a 1 t pod at 0.1-0.3 m/s can carry only 1-12 kg of net buoyancy before it stalls, and a stalled pod freezes into the ice cover at 1-2 cm/day. The repair uses 10 t broadside "fin" pods (5.0 × 2.2 × 1.2 m), soaked to 0 °C and trimmed in the launch slot with a crane load cell to +3 to +9 kg net buoyancy. That keeps drag (about 170 N at 0.16 m/s) larger than buoyancy, so pods dive under ice roughness instead of sticking. Routes are limited to reaches with smooth thermal ice and under-ice velocity of at least 0.2 m/s, mainly regulated rivers below hydropower dams (Kolyma, Vilyuy, Yenisei). An 8-10 cm shell survives transit (6 cm melt in 45 days), 700 km takes 41-68 days, and a pair of slots moves 1,200 t/day, or 144 kt per season.
value: Handling costs about $7.3/t including 5% lost pods, against $59-176/t by winter road over 500-1,500 km (8-24x cheaper) and 1.7-5x cheaper than summer barges, with coal as the best cargo.

label: erp2_b
name: Albedo-steered freeze-dry deflation placer
mech: Anchor kept: in spring, cold dry wind freeze-dries frozen pay gravel by sublimation and blows away the freed fines without any liquid water, leaving the heavies behind as a lag. An hourly energy-balance model for Pevek shows the claimed 0.4-0.7 mm w.e./day holds for only about 2 weeks. A dark surface begins melting around Apr 28 (7-24 mm/day of melt in May). The repair is to steer the albedo: keep the surface dark while it is cold, then leave the raked, lighter lag (albedo 0.3-0.55) once the surface nears 0 °C. This keeps the surface below 0 °C and gives 13 mm w.e. per season (48 days), times 0.6 for the dry-lag penalty (1 mm of dry grains halves the rate). That frees only 58-109 mm of gravel per year, depending on pore ice of 8-15%, so 100,000 m³/yr needs 0.9-1.4 km² of wind-scoured bench or dump surface. The site also needs a blade pass after each snowfall (spring snowfall of about 10 mm w.e. equals the whole budget), 0.6-1.4 m snow fences, and a low saltation-trap lip downwind. The trap is needed because gold flakes start moving at u* 0.23-0.32 m/s, the same as sand, although gold never goes into suspension (Stokes settling 0.6-6.6 m/s).
value: About $3.7-4.5 per m³ processed (about $8-9 per g recovered at 0.6 g/m³) against $6.0/m³ (about $12.5/g) for bulldozer-sluice washing, so 1.3-1.6x cheaper, not 3.6x; on old tailings it is only about 1x.

label: erp2_b
name: Self-feeding ore-ice buttress dam
mech: Anchor kept: the frozen ore pile holds the forebay water, and warm water run over its downstream face thaws it, so feed = flow × ΔT / thaw energy. The regime where this is strongest is a loose winter-hoisted pile (bulk ice 0.15, 50-55 MJ/m³). With creek or forebay water at 5-7 °C it needs 2.2-3.2 m³ of water per m³, which matches what a sluice needs (about 3 m³/m³). The original ice-cemented pile (101 MJ/m³) needs 3.8-8 m³/m³ and is water-limited. A loose pile leaks: its cold content refreezes only 5-16% of its voids. The repair is a 3 m upstream ore skin, spray-sealed in winter (a 0.4 m lift freezes in 10-19 h), under a 0.8-1 m saturated-peat blanket that thaws only 0.42 m in 90 days. The forebay is kept at 3 m or less (sliding safety factor about 5, Froehlich breach peak 34 m³/s against 144 m³/s for a season-long reservoir). Above 8-9 °C cold creek water is blended in, because the water ratio would otherwise fall below 2. The face can thaw about 70 m/day, against the 0.8 m/day needed.
value: Summer washing of winter-mined stockpiles costs about $2.0/m³ ($2.95/g at 0.8 g/m³) against about $4.65/m³ ($6.8/g) for natural thaw plus dozer ripping plus loader plus pumped sluice, or for hydromonitor plus gravel pump, so 2.3x cheaper (not 5x).

label: erp2_b
name: Drawdown-timed ice boulder lift
mech: Anchor kept: bottom-fast pond ice freezes onto the boulder tops and a spring water rise floats them off. The original timing (ice reaching the boulders in March) fails. The remaining 775 °C·days of frost freeze 39 cm of gravel onto the floe base, a load of 402 kg/m² against 141 kg/m² of buoyancy, so the floe stays grounded. The repair keeps the pond deeper than the ice until about Apr 25, then draws it down so the ice settles onto the boulders for the last 91 °C·days only. That freezes on only 4.4 cm of gravel, so 1.7 m natural ice lifts 0.058 m³/m² of stone and 3.2 m flood-built ice lifts 0.133 m³/m². A 0.8 m boulder needs 5-9 m² of floe to break out, so only a surface boulder armour of about 10-20% cover can be cleared, not boulders buried in the pay. Floating strips 30 × 100 m are sawn and winched into a dump bay.
value: About $5.1-5.7 per m³ of boulder against $2.7-3.0/m³ for a dozer push or excavator grapple on drained ground (about 0.5x), so it pays only where machines cannot reach, such as surface armour inside a flooded dredge pond.

label: erp2_b
name: Cold-sealed rolling snow-log pods
mech: Anchor kept: crushed ore plus snow sealed in an ice shell, carried by the current under winter river ice with no vessel and no return trip. The near-neutral +3 to +9 kg trim fails by orders of magnitude. Shell melt alone (the idea's own 6 cm) costs -196 kg of buoyancy. Snow at 250-350 kg/m³ creeps under hydrostatic load and loses 95-5,300 kg of buoyancy per day (Vionnet 2012 viscosity), and the trapped air gives 521 kg per metre of depth (a Cartesian-diver instability). The repair: a 1.6 m diameter rolling "log", snow pre-compacted to 550 kg/m³ (0.74 m³/t for coal, 1.6 for rock ore), sealed at -35 °C so it self-pressurises to +14.9 kPa, with a +750 kg margin. Creep then costs only 0.6-1.4% (about 100 kg) per 45 days. But rolling needs a mean under-ice velocity of 0.20-0.41 m/s, and getting past ice keels of 5-20 cm needs 0.62-0.95 m/s. Measured under-ice velocities are 0.05-0.25 m/s (Lena delta), and tailwater at +0.5 to +2 °C below dams melts the shell in 0.3-1.1 days.
value: If it ran, pods would cost about $6.8/t for coal against about $124/t by winter road and $27-33/t by summer barge plus stockpiling (4-5x cheaper than the barge), but no surveyed reach has the required velocity, so the ratio is moot.

label: erp2_a
name: Carbonyl nickel rides gas pipelines
mech: Anchor kept: nickel travels as Ni(CO)4 vapour in the Power of Siberia line's own gas flow (9.8 MPa, 38 bcm/yr) and is split back out at the Amur gas plant where the line ends. Repaired design: 0.027 mol% carries 25 kt Ni/yr, which is Kun-Manie scale. That dose is at a saturation ratio of 0.25 at -10 °C. Compressor discharge is capped at 45 °C, so only 0.035% CO is needed to keep the carbonyl stable (the original 0.15% was sized for 80 °C). At the plant, a cold-oil absorber (20-60 kg/s of oil, 10-16 stages) catches 99.999% and leaves 2.7 ppb in sales gas, instead of heating the whole 879 kg/s stream (423 MW gross). The concentrated carbonyl is then decomposed at 200 °C. Propane hydrate does not apply here; the binding cost is CO make-up of 2.53 t CO per t Ni (about $514/t Ni).
value: The physics works, but the pipeline leg costs about $960/t Ni more than running the same carbonyl refinery at the BAM/PoS junction and shipping pellets by rail, which saves only $27/t Ni of freight (about 0.03x). The whole chain at $6.6-8.4k/t Ni is no cheaper than selling concentrate at 70-75% payability ($5.4-6.1k/t Ni lost), so it FAILS on cost.

label: erp2_a
name: Freeze-Engine Vitriol Winning
mech: Anchor kept: freezing the stored copper leach liquor runs a Rankine engine that rejects heat to Arctic air, and the same freezing crystallises CuSO4·5H2O. Repairs: (1) The direct-contact refrigerant changes from propane to n-butane. Propane boiling at -6 to -8 °C (3.5-3.9 bar) sits inside the propane-hydrate field. (2) Fan power is now counted: 8.7 kJ per kg of ice against 15.2 gross at -40 °C. The fans are replaced by a natural-draft dry tower. (3) Integrated over a real Yakutsk November-March winter, the engine nets 7.6 kJ per kg of ice. That covers 50% of electrowinning power at 2.5 g/L, not 80-104%. (4) Freezing costs $1.5-2.5 per m³ of feed, so dilute liquor loses. The process is moved to 10-15 g/L liquor from leach-solution recycle on siliceous low-Mg oxide ore (Mg ≤ 2 g/L, Fe ≤ 1 g/L, since impurities concentrate 24x). There it needs 77-117 kg of ice per kg Cu, and the engine supplies 8-12% of electrowinning power.
value: $1,222-1,379/t Cu against $1,590/t Cu for diesel-powered solvent extraction plus electrowinning (1.15-1.3x cheaper), but it loses to grid-powered SX-EW ($1,086/t). NICHE.

label: erp2_a
name: Self-Charging Frost Separator Cascade
mech: Anchor kept: grains charged on the chute lining build the separating field themselves, through bins cross-wired to the opposite plates, with no power supply. The stated 30 kV/m gives only 4-9 cm of drift (not 30-60) and is space-charge-limited to 0.15 t/h per metre, which would need 7 km of plates. Repaired design: - A 0.3 m gap self-excites to 90 kV (300 kV/m, 8% of breakdown at -40 °C). That gives 41 cm of drift over a 1.5 m fall and 1.47 t/h per metre, or about 700 m of plates in total for 1 Mt/yr. - Insulating grains cannot hand over charge the way water drops do in a Kelvin dropper. Instead, discharges inside the charged grain pile pass about 98% of it to the bin. Leakage must stay above 2.2e10 Ω per metre. - Intake air must be heated to 20-40 °C, not 0 °C, to dry ore with 1-2% moisture: 137 MJ/t against 43-54 MJ/t of mill heat.
value: $3,994/t Li2O delivered against $4,588 for dense-media separation plus haul (the best baseline, 1.15x) and $6,292 for Arctic flotation (1.6x). NICHE.

label: erp2_a
name: Night-sky lithium freeze cascade
mech: Anchor tested: trays radiating through the 8-13 µm window push Ca-Li brine below the CaCl2-ice eutectic (-49.8 °C) so Ca locks up and LiCl stays liquid. My own band model agrees with the original: - With no brine load the film settles 8.1 K below -40 °C air. - A film at -52 °C cools only when the air is at -45 °C or colder. That is 288 hours a winter, freezing 36 kg per m². - So the trays need 13,000-35,600 m² per t LCE per year (Udachnaya brine averages 147 mg/L Li). Keeping the anchor above the eutectic does not help: crystallising CaCl2·6H2O from brines with 36-40% CaCl2 needs only plain -40 °C air (Li concentrates x1.3-1.9), and radiative trays add only x1.81 to x1.92. Only niche: freeze-concentrate Ca-free sorbent eluate in thin flooded layers with -40 °C air (about 100 m² per t LCE), which drops the anchor.
value: As stated, at least $65-178k/t LCE against $3.4-6.2k for the whole sorption route, so it FAILS. The eluate niche beats RO plus mechanical evaporation ($690-1,150/t LCE on diesel) only off-grid; on grid power that route costs $260-440/t LCE.

label: rt_b
name: Sun-face windrow freeze-dry placer
mech: Anchor kept: sun and wind sublimate the ice cement of frozen pay with no liquid water, and wind carries off the freed fines while gold stays. In the repaired design, drained pay is piled in autumn into windrows with 37° south faces (~0.06 pore ice instead of 0.15-0.30). The faces shed snow, clear themselves of loose grains, and get 2.6x the irradiance of flat ground. Sorting no longer relies on a threshold window. The saltating sand and any mobile gold (up to ~100-200 µm) settle in the trough between ridges. Only the suspended fraction leaves the site: quartz finer than 63-97 µm and gold finer than 23-35 µm. An hourly energy balance for Tiksi gives a face sublimation of 0.08-0.13 kg/m²/day in March and 0.41-0.67 in April 1-20. The window closes on Apr 20 because faces reach -2 °C or warmer after that. A 0.5 mm dry skin halves the rate and a 3 mm lag cuts it 6x. The season totals 5.2 kg/m², so faces retreat only 0.02-0.09 m.
value: 100,000 m³/yr needs about 0.9 km² raked daily or 213 km of ridges, at $4.4-12.1/m³ ($7.4-20.3/g) against $1.7-6.0/m³ ($2.9-10.1/g) for conventional washing. That is about 0.5x, so it costs more, and only a small niche at waterless sites remains.

label: rt_b
name: Solar-pond self-dosing ore pile
mech: Anchor kept: the frozen ore pile feeds itself. Warm water thaws its face at a rate set by flow × water temperature, so the feed needs no dozer. Two changes from the original: the 1-2 mm film spread over a 40-100 m face is replaced by a channel along the toe of the face, and the ore pile no longer holds back water. In the toe channel, 47-100 L/s at a slope of 0.05-0.08 gives 30-57 Pa of shear, which clears clasts finer than 42-78 mm. The water gives up its heat within e-folding lengths of 10-31 m, so feed still equals flow × heat. Water comes by gravity from a lined solar pond, 0.4 m deep and 0.7-1.5 ha, that warms the creek by 4-6 K. Season output is about 123,000 m³ with the pond, against 54,500 m³ from a 4 °C creek. A fixed weir bypass keeps the chute at 4 m³ of water per m³ or more, while the face alone swings from 2.4 to 12.1. A grizzly and a loader (2-3 h a day) remove the oversize.
value: Feed dozing, ripping and pumping drop out of the washing stage at winter-mined placers. Per recovered gram this is only 1.03-1.13x cheaper than today's stockpile thawing and dozer feed.

label: rt_b
name: Ice-lift oversize boulder clean-up
mech: Anchor kept: pond ice freezes onto stones and the spring rise floats the ice off with the stones in it. The design now uses a gap: water depth is set so the ice bottom stays at least 0.3 m above the mined pit floor in 99% of winters. With the snow ploughed off, ice is 1.8 ± 0.08 m and the depth is 2.12 m. The floor never freezes and no gold-bearing matrix is caught. Only oversize (over 1.2 m) left standing on the floor after the gravel is mined is gripped, with P ≈ 1.00. Ploughed spring ice gives 101-126 kg/m² of net lift, so a 1.5 m boulder needs 21-31 m² of floe. Adfreeze grip margins are 1.6-4.9x for 1.5 m boulders but only 0.6-1.8x for 2.5 m boulders, which caps the method at about 2 m. The pond sits below grade in the mined-out pit, so there is no dam, and floes are winched from shore.
value: Clearing oversize by ice costs about $2-2.5/m³ of boulder against $4-8/m³ for secondary blasting, about 2-3x cheaper for the oversize alone. That is only 0.04-2.5% of the cost per recovered gram, so it is a niche.

label: rt_b
name: Short-haul trimmed under-ice ore pods
mech: Anchor kept: crushed ore or coal and snow sealed in an ice shell drift with the current under winter ice, with no vessel and no return trip. The rigid ice shell is essential: in a flexible bag, a 0.7 m change in ice draft would change buoyancy by 390 kg. An HDPE skid on top (μ 0.15, assumed) widens the trim window to 90-404 kg. Pods are filled in autumn at -4 °C, which adds only +10 kg of cold-reserve buoyancy against +65 kg for contents at -25 °C, so no open soaking slot is needed. Pods are 1.2 m tall with a 7-13 cm shell. At 3.7, 11 or 18.4 kg/day of buoyancy loss (water +0.01, +0.03 or +0.05 K), usable trips are only 76-428 km. Coal pods carry 8 t with flooded voids and a 1.76 m³ snow pocket. Routes run in early winter (ice 0.6-1.0 m, so 1.75-2.1 m of depth is needed), more than 1,400 km below the Kolyma dam polynya, and deliver to consumers that burn the cargo in winter. The test case is Zyryanka coal to Srednekolymsk, about 330 km, with roughly 327 m³/s and 0.18-0.33 m/s under the ice.
value: Estimated at $10-20/t delivered, against $39/t by winter road over the same 330 km (1.9-3.9x) and $12-37/t by summer barge plus a stockpile (0.6-3.7x). That is not the 8-24x claimed, and it is unproven.

label: rt_a
name: Carbonyl nickel rides gas pipelines
mech: Anchor kept: nickel travels as Ni(CO)4 vapour (0.04 mol%) inside a trunk gas line's own flow and is split back to metal where the line ends. Injection now goes in only downstream of the last local offtake. Before any planned vent, injection stops for one transit time (10 h per 300 km, 72 h for the full 2,159 km at 8.3 m/s) and Gazprom's mobile compressor units pump the section down, so planned vents release almost no carbonyl. Compressor discharge is capped at 50 °C, which cuts the CO stabiliser from 0.15% to 0.05% (equilibrium needs 0.032%), so CO use falls from 3.70 to 2.51 t per t Ni, against a hard minimum of 1.91. A 250 °C nickel-bed polisher after the decomposer leaves 0.09 ppb Ni(CO)4 in the sales gas at equilibrium (4.5 ppb at 200 °C). Unsolved: a rupture still releases about 12 t Ni(CO)4 per 30 km section, which is 8.8e8 m³ of air at the IDLH. Its 40-60 s half-life in air means only 0.3-2% survives 1 km downwind, but CO in the plume can slow the breakdown to minutes.
value: The pipeline-specific cost is $109-947/t Ni (one-way CO plus lost line capacity, minus the CO's value as fuel), against about $100-150/t Ni to ship pellets or matte, so it loses to best practice unless CO is a free by-product costing under about $56/t; it beats only trucking concentrate ($1,067/t Ni), by 0.8-1.9x.

label: rt_a
name: Freeze-Engine Vitriol Winning
mech: Anchor kept: freezing stored copper leach liquor both drives a heat engine (the heat of freezing boils the working fluid, which condenses in Arctic air) and crystallises CuSO4·5H2O. Propane is replaced by n-butane, which forms no hydrate on its own and was the direct-contact fluid in the 1960s-70s secondary-refrigerant freeze-desalination pilots. It boils at 0.87-0.97 bar against the liquor and condenses at 0.19-0.30 bar. Freezing is staged so that most ice forms while the liquor is still dilute, which keeps the ice-weighted freezing point at -0.8 °C. Copper recovery is capped at 80% and feed acid at 2.5 g/L, and the 90% case is dropped. Fans would eat about half the output, so a 60-80 m natural-draft dry tower (47-52 Pa of draft at -35 °C) replaces them, and freezing is scheduled into the coldest hours. That gives 6-9 kJ per kg of ice, enough for 42-63% of electrowinning power at Udachny-type cold but only 24-44% at Chara (Udokan). A richer 10 g/L leach solution cuts ice from 492 to 123 kg per kg Cu and the freeze step to $105-165/t Cu, but then the engine covers only about 12% of electrowinning power.
value: At 2.5 g/L the route is 0.56-0.86x as cheap as grid-powered SX-EW at Udokan (i.e. dearer) and 0.83-1.08x at an off-grid diesel site; only an off-grid, low-Mg, 10 g/L case reaches about 1.1-1.4x cheaper.

label: rt_a
name: Self-Charging Frost Separator Cascade
mech: Anchor kept: grains charge themselves on the chute lining, and the bins that catch them, wired across to the opposite plates, build the separating field with no power supply, like a Kelvin water dropper. The field is reset to 150 kV/m across a 0.5 m gap (75 kV, 5% of air breakdown), which gives 17-23 cm of drift per side in a drag-included simulation without grains hitting the plates (200 kV/m would hit them). The sorted charge delivers only 0.4-1.4 µA per metre of plate width, so self-excitation needs at least 5e10 Ω of leakage resistance per 10 m channel. Space charge caps each channel at 0.17-0.5 t/h per metre of plate width, so each stage is a stack of alternating-polarity plates at 0.5 m pitch: 170-525 channels, each 10 m wide, for 1 Mt/yr. Ore moisture is removed by a closed air loop through an outdoor cold trap at -30 °C, which gives 2% RH at the separator. Mill heat and diesel-generator waste heat supply the drying heat: 9-19 MJ/t at 0.2-0.4% ice, 47 MJ/t at 1% ice. With middlings recycled, eight stages reach 6.2% Li2O at 82% recovery only if each stage sends forward 85% of the spodumene and 45% of the waste. A 80/50 split needs 22 stages and 23x circulating load, and a 75/55 split cannot reach 6% at all.
value: $4,100-4,960 per t of Li2O recovered at the railhead, against $6,430-7,390 for XRT sorting plus DMS (the cheapest real alternative) and $7,400-8,270 for Arctic DMS plus flotation, so 1.3-1.8x cheaper, and only if a measured per-stage split of 85/45 or better holds.

label: rt_a
name: Night-sky lithium freeze cascade
mech: The anchor (night-sky cooling that drives CaCl2 brine below its -50 °C eutectic) cannot be rescued. Even with a heat pump rejecting to -40/-45 °C air, it needs 5.5-15 MWh per t LCE and must freeze 450-910 t of brine per t LCE, and the leftover liquor is still about 30% CaCl2, so DLE is still needed. Above the eutectic, cold concentrates lithium only 1.25x. The surviving niche keeps only "Arctic cold concentrates lithium" and applies it to Ca-free sorbent eluate. Reverse osmosis first takes the eluate to 6 g/L Li (37 bar osmotic pressure). Two stages of spray freezing (snowmaking guns rather than trays) then take it to 20.6 g/L by draining the unfrozen brine and collecting the early melt. That moves 53% of the Li per pass, needs 62 t of ice per t LCE, and gives a product that freezes at -14 °C. Late melt at ≤1.1 g/L Li goes back to the RO feed, so no lithium is lost in the ice, and winter-only freezing needs 0.37 Mm³ of stored RO concentrate, not 2.2-7.3 Mm³.
value: $110-240/t LCE against $470-1,085/t LCE for the MVR evaporator it replaces (2-4x cheaper for that step), but that is only 5-15% off the $3.4-6.2k/t LCE whole route, and the night-sky/eutectic anchor is not used.

label: gx_front_1
name: Plume-Assay Needle Drilling
mech: A sled-mounted ~100 kW gyrotron (CAP 24) vaporises a finger-thin hole through frozen overburden and ore with no bit, rods or drilling fluid, so permafrost never thaws and no water or core is hauled. A nitrogen purge lifts the rock vapour; a spectrometer reads its atomic emission lines every few centimetres, and the condensed fume is bagged as a check sample. The rig steps across a coarse grid and adds holes wherever the plume chemistry spikes.
value: Remote deposits gain bankable grade and tonnage at a fraction of the cost and time of core drilling with fly-out assays.

label: gx_front_1
name: Robot-Built Self-Dredging Rivers
mech: Each winter, autonomous excavators that scan, grasp and stack irregular boulders without mortar (CAP 20) work the dry bars and frozen bed of a shallow tributary between deposit and navigable river, building dry-stone wing dams that pinch every riffle. The spring flood, squeezed through the gaps, scours a deep continuous channel that shallow-draft barges use all summer. After each flood the robots re-scan the bed and lengthen, raise or notch walls where scour fell short or overshot.
value: Hundreds of kilometres of unused small rivers become maintained freight waterways for a fraction of a road's cost.

label: gx_front_1
name: Tuned-Burst Frozen Ground Ripping
mech: Lithotripsy-style transducer arrays (CAP 23), coupled to a frozen face through a brine film, fire ultrasound bursts tuned to the grain size of ice-cemented gravel or silt, so the weak ice bonds between grains fatigue and fail while the stones stay whole. A light loader scrapes off each loosened, still-frozen layer, and burst frequency is retuned as scanned grain size changes. Unheated rigs run through polar night on sodium-ion packs that keep over 90% capacity at −40 °C (CAP 9).
value: Frozen overburden and ore are dug year-round by small electric machines, without explosives or waiting for summer thaw.

label: gx_front_1
name: Fusion-Magnet Dry Kimberlite Rejection
mech: A 20-tesla REBCO coil (CAP 6) stands at the pit rim, its cryocooler dumping heat into winter air. Crushed dry kimberlite falls through its open field gradient: iron- and magnesium-silicate grains are dragged sideways, while diamagnetic diamonds and non-magnetic grains drop straight into a small product stream. Splitter vanes are reset continuously from X-ray diamond counts in each stream.
value: Most kimberlite is rejected dry at the pit, shrinking the heated wet plant and its ore haulage several-fold.

label: gx_front_1
name: Self-Levelling Pressure-Cell Foundations
mech: Modular plants and camps rest on mats of Vectran-strap pressure cells (CAP 21), flown in folded, that spread load over untouched tundra so ground pressure stays below what the active layer bears. Tilt sensors drive a small compressor that inflates or bleeds individual cells as ice-rich ground settles or heaves, keeping structures level for decades.
value: Facilities go onto raw permafrost in days, skipping pile rigs, freeze-back waits and gravel pads.

label: gx_fl_2
name: Thaw-scored slab toppling
mech: Hot-water jet holes thaw thin slots that score frozen overburden, base included, into slabs ~10 m tall and 3 m thick. Woven Vectran cushions from inflatable space habitats (CAP 21), slid into the back slot and inflated below 1 bar, tip each ~450 t slab into the previous mined-out strip, letting gravity move it. A site model stores hole spacing against measured ice content and retunes it after every topple.
value: Strips frozen overburden using about a tenth of today's dozer-hours and diesel per gram.

label: gx_fl_2
name: Black-sand-steered bedrock moles
mech: Battery robots cut drifts along bedrock under intact frozen overburden left as roof, removing only the 1-1.5 m gold layer. Quantum magnetometers built for GPS-free navigation (CAP 4) serve as ore-ahead sensors: magnetite black sand travels with gold, so robots steer up the magnetic gradient and store a 3D pay map. Sodium-ion packs working at −40 °C (CAP 9) emit no exhaust heat, so winter air ventilates the drifts without thawing the roof.
value: Ends stripping, cutting volume moved and diesel per gram of placer gold about tenfold.

label: gx_fl_2
name: Coal micro-pits beside settlements
mech: A sled-towed cold-atom gravity gradiometer built to find tunnels (CAP 5) maps shallow coal lenses, half as dense as host rock, near Lena-basin settlements. An autonomous excavator, its dry-stone vision and grasping (CAP 20) retrained to sort frozen coal from rock, mines a few thousand tonnes unattended each winter. Lens rankings and measured ash are stored and updated, so the robot backfills and moves on.
value: A short winter haul replaces hundreds of kilometres of barge and winter road, cutting settlement coal logistics about tenfold.

label: gx_fl_2
name: Flash-distilled lithium at the pit
mech: Crushed pegmatite plus a chloride donor gets a one-second flash Joule pulse (CAP 15), repurposed as a still that boils lithium off as LiCl. Staged condensers catch alkali chlorides hot and Fe/Al chlorides cold; soda ash precipitates Li2CO3 and freed NaCl is recycled. Thermophotovoltaic cells lining the chamber (CAP 7) recapture up to a third of pulse energy; pulse length is retuned from each batch's logged Li:Na condensate ratio.
value: Containerised flash lines replace concentrator, kiln and acid-leach plant, cutting process capital per tonne LCE about tenfold.

label: gx_fl_2
name: Woven lay-flat crude line
mech: A 100 mm lay-flat hose jacketed in the Vectran strapping of inflatable space habitats (CAP 21) is unreeled by a tracked vehicle along the existing winter road, with no trench or piles. Crude-fired pump skids every ~15 km move the field's ~27 m³/h, dosing pour-point depressant and setting speed from line temperature and pressure. Skid-to-skid mass balance locates leaks; the hose is rewound and reused when the field declines.
value: Turns ~$10/bbl trucking into about $1/bbl, so 300 km tie-ins of small East-Siberian fields to ESPO pay.

label: gx_front_2
name: Ore stream as heat battery
mech: Crushed gold-quartz ore waits weeks in insulated silos, charged with cheap surplus electricity to ~600 °C like the soapstone heat battery (CAP 10), then discharged through air loops to heat camp and plant through winter. Each cycle drives quartz through its 573 °C inversion, whose sudden volume jump microcracks grain boundaries, so the cooled ore grinds far more easily and releases its gold. Charging is scheduled by heat demand and power price.
value: One kilowatt-hour pays twice, covering an Arctic mine's two largest energy bills: heating and grinding.

label: gx_front_2
name: Grinding mill brews its lixiviant
mech: Copper-nickel ore is dry-ground in steel-ball mills under nitrogen-hydrogen gas, so freshly abraded iron from balls and liners fixes ammonia at ~45 °C and 1 bar (CAP 14). The ammonia-rich off-gas feeds an ammoniacal leach that dissolves metals from the just-ground ore as ammine complexes; ammonia is stripped, recycled and topped up by the mill. Hydrogen comes from on-site electrolysis, and the gas mix is tuned to ore sulphur content.
value: The plant runs on power, air and water alone, ending inbound reagent convoys.

label: gx_front_2
name: Resonant kimberlite unmaking
mech: Kimberlite lumps cross a water bath swept by burst-wave ultrasound of the kind that grinds kidney stones through skin (CAP 23), its frequency stepped up as fragments shrink. Stress amplitude exceeds altered kimberlite's tensile strength but stays about a hundred times below diamond's, so the matrix turns to sand while diamonds pass unbroken. Sand is screened off, leaving a small heavy residue for sorting.
value: A containerised, crusher-free plant processes kimberlite and recovers large stones whole.

label: gx_front_2
name: Flash-unlocked refractory gold
mech: Arsenopyrite concentrate, conductive enough to need no carbon additive, receives one-second current pulses to ~3,000 °C (CAP 15) that destroy the sulphide lattice locking invisible gold and drive arsenic into a cold trap. The porous calcine is leached in dilute chloride, and a whey-protein amyloid aerogel (CAP 18) adsorbs the gold selectively; the loaded sponge is burned to doré. Pulse energy is tuned per batch to measured sulphur and arsenic.
value: Stranded refractory gold deposits become treatable by a flown-in, cyanide-free container instead of a pressure-oxidation plant.

label: gx_front_2
name: Supply drones survey while flying
mech: Cargo drones on 500 Wh/kg cells (CAP 8) resupply remote camps, navigating by quantum magnetometers against crustal-field maps (CAP 4) where satellite navigation is jammed. The map-mismatch residuals that navigation normally discards are logged with inertial positions and fused into a steadily sharpening anomaly map. Residual patterns resembling kimberlite pipes or magnetite skarns automatically route the next flight lower over them.
value: Exploration of roadless Siberia becomes a free by-product of routine logistics.

label: gx_fl_1
name: Robot drift-mining under frozen roof
mech: Instead of stripping 5-15 m of frozen overburden, an autonomous excavator tunnels only the 1-2 m pay gravel on bedrock, using the frozen ground above as roof. Its sodium-ion pack (CAP 9) works at −40°C and emits no exhaust heat, so the roof stays frozen. Its dry-stone-walling autonomy (CAP 20) stacks cobbles into mortarless pillars behind the face and re-plans spans from face scans, so no pay is left in pillars.
value: Moves 5-10x less ground per gram, attacking earthmoving, about two-thirds of physical placer cost.

label: gx_fl_1
name: Woven pressure-shell concentrator
mech: Flotation cells, tanks, thickener walls and the building envelope are Vectran-strap woven shells (CAP 21) holding slurry instead of cabin air: 6 m of slurry is 0.8 bar, about a sixth of demonstrated burst. They ship folded and sit on insulated gravel pads, needing no piles, structural steel or welders; only rotors and pumps are rigid, and cells are added as throughput grows.
value: Turns the steel, piling and erection core of a 41% capital share into a one-summer flat-pack build at about a tenth of the cost.

label: gx_fl_1
name: Floating bluff coal miner
mech: Many river settlements sit near bluffs where coal seams outcrop. A self-propelled barge with an autonomous excavator works the bluff nearest each settlement during the navigation season, cutting frozen coal into its hold, unloading at the riverside yard, then moving to the next exposure. Its dry-stone-walling autonomy (CAP 20) re-stacks the removed rock slabs as a mortarless revetment, so the cut bank cannot thaw and slump.
value: Replaces a 1,000-2,000 km barge-plus-winter-road chain with a 10-100 km haul, cutting settlement coal's 85% logistics share about tenfold.

label: gx_fl_1
name: Flash-and-electrolyse lithium containers
mech: One-second Joule pulses (CAP 15), designed for rare-earth fly ash, flip carbon-mixed spodumene concentrate into an acid-leachable phase without a kiln. An ambient-temperature electrolyser (CAP 16), designed for cement, splits recycled sodium sulphate into sulphuric acid that leaches the lithium and caustic that purifies it into hydroxide, regenerating the sulphate. With no acid plant or bulk reagent imports, containers supplied by winter road replace the converter.
value: Removes most of a 91 bn rub plant and the 40 bn rub all-season road, cutting a 42% capital share several- to tenfold.

label: gx_fl_1
name: Superconducting rotating-field grinding pipe
mech: Polyphase rotating-field coils (CAP 11), built for truck charging, are wound with REBCO tape (CAP 6), built for fusion, around a stationary non-magnetic pipe. The field whirls loose steel needles through the ore slurry so they collide and grind it; field speed is tuned to the measured product size, and capacity grows by adding pipe sections. There is no rotating shell, girth gear, liner or 1,000-t foundation.
value: Makes grinding, the heaviest and most foundation-hungry block of a porphyry concentrator's capital, roughly ten times lighter to build on permafrost.

label: gx_ledg_2
name: Jacked Frozen-Block Stripping
mech: Overlapping hot-water-drilled holes cut frozen overburden into 20×20 m blocks, and summer creek water injected at bedrock thaws only the gold-bearing gravel beneath one block. Hydraulic jacks bracing against the next frozen block push the ~8,000-t block into the previously mined cell, exposing the thawed paystreak for excavator and sluice. Blocks advance downstream like sliding-puzzle tiles; kerf spacing adapts to measured ice content.
value: Overburden is pushed rather than ripped, using about 0.1 l diesel/m³ instead of ~1 l/m³, cutting placer earthmoving roughly tenfold.

label: gx_ledg_2
name: Bell-Hole Thaw-Lift Mining
mech: A tracked sonic rig drills cased 0.3 m holes on a 6 m grid through frozen overburden. At bedrock a rotating hot-water jet thaws a 3 m-radius bell of paystreak, an airlift raises the slurry to a sluice, and tailings return to backfill the bell and refreeze, while frozen roof and pillars stand. Jetting time adapts to the gold grade of the returning slurry.
value: Under 1% of overburden is disturbed, cutting fuel from ~11 to ~2 l diesel/g and opening placers too deep to strip.

label: gx_ledg_2
name: Village Coal-Slurry Wells
mech: Where coal-bearing strata lie beneath or beside a settlement, boreholes reach the seam, a warm-water jet cuts the frozen coal and an airlift lifts the slurry. The slurry is milled and thickened into coal-water fuel and pumped a few hundred metres into a retrofitted boiler, so the coal is never dried, barged, stockpiled or trucked. Wells are added as cavities exhaust.
value: For settlements on coal-bearing ground, it removes the barge and winter-road haulage that makes up ~85% of boiler-gate coal cost.

label: gx_ledg_2
name: Snow-Bedded Seasonal Crude Hose
mech: Each November a reel-sled lays a 300-km polyurethane lay-flat hose along the winter-road route and a groomer buries it in compacted snow, which supports and insulates it; associated-gas-fired booster pumps keep light crude moving. The field produces its whole annual volume in the five winter months and is shut in over summer, so the reservoir itself is the storage tank. In April the hose is purged with nitrogen, reeled and reused.
value: Replaces ~$10/bbl trucking with roughly $2-3/bbl for small stranded East-Siberian fields, with no permanent pipeline.

label: gx_ledg_2
name: Flooded-Pit Floating Mine
mech: After a starter cut the porphyry pit is flooded, and under winter ice its water stays a few degrees above freezing. Benches are drilled and blasted from barges or the ice, a cutter-suction dredge pumps broken ore to a concentrator built from barge modules floating on the same lake, and tailings settle into mined-out depths behind the dredge. Dredging depth and blast pattern follow the block model as the lake deepens.
value: Eliminates the haul fleet, roads, crushers, dewatering, tailings dam and heated foundations, roughly halving capital, the largest cost of Arctic copper.

label: gx_ledg_1
name: Highwall-Mined Frozen Paystreaks
mech: One trench is cut along the placer valley to bedrock; from it a remote-controlled coal highwall miner bores parallel 1.5 m entries 300 m sideways along the bedrock contact, taking only the gold-bearing gravel. The frozen overburden, as strong as weak rock, stands unsupported as roof between narrow pillars and is never stripped. Gravel is cut year-round, stockpiled and washed in summer.
value: Earthmoving and diesel per gram fall roughly 8-10x, removing about half of placer delivered cost and opening deep-overburden placers.

label: gx_ledg_1
name: Village Coal Gasified Underfoot
mech: Where a settlement sits on coal-bearing strata, as across much of the Lena basin, directional wells from its boiler-house yard reach the seam, are linked, and gasify it in place with injected air and steam. Tar-stripped syngas fires the existing boilers through new gas burners; a 10 kt/yr village consumes under half a hectare of seam a year, so one new well pair every few years suffices.
value: The barge-plus-winter-road chain, about 85% of delivered fuel cost, disappears, making settlement heat roughly three times cheaper.

label: gx_ledg_1
name: Spodumene Through Nepheline Alumina Kilns
mech: Spodumene concentrate is blended into kiln feed at Russia's existing nepheline-limestone sinter alumina plants (Achinsk, Pikalyovo); at 1,250°C the lime opens spodumene as in the old lime-roast lithium process, and its alumina joins plant output. Dissolved lithium is caught by steps already running: it co-precipitates as lithium-aluminium hydroxide during CO2 carbonation or crystallizes as carbonate in the soda-potash evaporators. Only a small strip-and-purify circuit is new.
value: Lithium carbonate capacity for roughly a tenth of a greenfield chemical plant's capital, the largest cost term.

label: gx_ledg_1
name: Shipyard-Built Floating Concentrator Fleet
mech: Crushing, grinding and flotation are built as 10 Mt/yr barge modules in an ordinary shipyard at normal productivity, towed by river or sea in summer into a dredged basin beside the deposit, and moored in water kept open by process heat and bubblers. Floating eliminates piles, heated halls and site-built civil works on permafrost. When the orebody is exhausted, the modules are towed to the next deposit.
value: Escaping the 2-3x Far North build premium and reusing hulls across two or three deposits cuts capital per tonne roughly 5-8x.

label: gx_ledg_1
name: Mast-Hung Coal Belt to Okhotsk
mech: A rope-supported belt conveyor, its carriage rolling on steel track ropes strung between masts 100-200 m apart, carries South Yakutian coal about 450 km over the Dzhugdzhur range to an Okhotsk Sea jetty. It touches permafrost only at mast footings, spans rivers and gullies without bridges, needs no embankment, and regenerates power on descents, with cold-rated belts running year-round.
value: Moving 20-30 Mt/yr at about $5-8/t instead of a ~$46/t rail tariff removes most of the export chain's largest cost.
